You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution;
15	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
16	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
17	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
18	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
19	  execution;
20	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
21	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
22	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
23	  execution with reason `rejected`);
24	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
25	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
26	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
27	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
28	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
29	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
30	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
31	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
32	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
33	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
34	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
35	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
36	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
37	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
38	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
39	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
40	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
41	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
42	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
43	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
44	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
45	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
46	
47	## Requirements
48	
49	- Python 3.11 or newer
50	- no third-party runtime dependencies
51	
52	## Run the service
53	
54	```bash
55	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
56	```
57	
58	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
59	has bound the port.
60	
61	## HTTP API
62	
63	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
64	
65	### Tenants and quotas
66	
67	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
68	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
69	and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
70	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
71	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
72	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
73	example advancing, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
74	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
75	workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
76	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
77	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
78	workflow of the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier is the
79	usual `404 not_found`.
80	
81	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
82	including creation, advancement, approval decisions, lease operations,
83	cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status queries. An empty
84	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
85	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
86	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
87	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
88	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
89	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
90	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
91	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
92	the usual `409 conflict`.
93	
94	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
95	hold:
96	
97	```http
98	PUT /quotas
99	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
100	X-Tenant-Id: acme
101	
102	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
103	```
104	
105	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
106	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
107	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
108	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
109	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
110	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
111	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
112	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
113	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
114	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
115	
116	```http
117	GET /quotas
118	X-Tenant-Id: acme
119	```
120	
121	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
122	when the tenant has declared none.
123	
124	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
125	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
126	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
127	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
128	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
129	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
130	
131	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
132	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
133	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
134	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
135	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
136	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
137	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
138	
139	### Health
140	
141	```http
142	GET /health
143	```
144	
145	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
146	
147	### Create a workflow
148	
149	```http
150	POST /workflows
151	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
152	
153	{
154	  "id": "order-flow",
155	  "nodes": [
156	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
157	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
158	  ]
159	}
160	```
161	
162	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
163	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
164	
165	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
166	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
167	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
168	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
169	
170	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
171	
172	```json
173	{
174	  "id": "order-flow",
175	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
176	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
177	}
178	```
179	
180	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
181	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
182	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
183	
184	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
185	
186	```json
187	{
188	  "id": "nightly-orders",
189	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
190	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
191	}
192	```
193	
194	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
195	
196	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
197	
198	```json
199	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
200	```
201	
202	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
203	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
204	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
205	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
206	`false`.
207	
208	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
209	
210	```json
211	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
212	```
213	
214	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
215	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
216	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
217	dependencies of its successors.
218	
219	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
220	
221	```json
222	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
223	```
224	
225	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
226	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
227	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
228	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
229	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
230	`retries_exhausted`.
231	
232	A task may instead declare an approval point:
233	
234	```json
235	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
236	```
237	
238	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
239	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
240	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
241	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
242	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
243	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
244	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
245	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
246	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
247	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
248	move the task.
249	
250	### Submit an approval decision
251	
252	```http
253	POST /executions/run-1/decision
254	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
255	
256	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
257	```
258	
259	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
260	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
261	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
262	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
263	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
264	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
265	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
266	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
267	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
268	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
269	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
270	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
271	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
272	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
273	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
274	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
275	404.
276	
277	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
278	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
279	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
280	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
281	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
282	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
283	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
284	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
285	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
286	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
287	shape and event stream.
288	
289	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
290	segment:
291	
292	```json
293	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
294	```
295	
296	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
297	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
298	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
299	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the entry task plus every node
300	reachable from it through `depends_on`; the body keeps the usual DAG rules and
301	must contain the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
302	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
303	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
304	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
305	loop node instead).
306	
307	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
308	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
309	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
310	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
311	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
312	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
313	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
314	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
315	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
316	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
317	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
318	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors.
319	
320	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
321	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
322	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
323	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
324	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
325	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
326	exactly.
327	
328	### Workflow versions
329	
330	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
331	
332	```json
333	{
334	  "id": "order-flow",
335	  "version": "2026-09-25",
336	  "nodes": [
337	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
338	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
339	  ]
340	}
341	```
342	
343	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
344	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
345	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
346	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
347	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
348	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
349	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
350	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
351	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
352	
353	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
354	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
355	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
356	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
357	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
358	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
359	
360	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
361	current version at the moment it starts:
362	
363	```http
364	POST /executions
365	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
366	
367	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
368	```
369	
370	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
371	
372	```json
373	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
374	```
375	
376	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
377	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
378	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
379	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
380	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
381	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
382	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
383	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
384	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
385	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
386	conclusions never change.
387	
388	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
389	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
390	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
391	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
392	stream with no added field.
393	
394	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
395	
396	```http
397	GET /workflows/order-flow
398	```
399	
400	```json
401	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
402	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
403	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
404	]}
405	```
406	
407	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
408	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
409	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
410	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
411	resources as usual.
412	
413	### Start an execution
414	
415	```http
416	POST /executions
417	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
418	
419	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
420	```
421	
422	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
423	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
424	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
425	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
426	
427	An execution may declare a timeout:
428	
429	```json
430	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
431	```
432	
433	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
434	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
435	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
436	a timeout never expire.
437	
438	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
439	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
440	
441	```json
442	{
443	  "id": "run-3",
444	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
445	  "input": {},
446	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
447	}
448	```
449	
450	### Inspect an execution
451	
452	```http
453	GET /executions/run-1
454	GET /executions/run-1/events
455	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
456	```
457	
458	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
459	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
460	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
461	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
462	
463	### Webhook notifications
464	
465	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
466	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
467	
468	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
469	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
470	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
471	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
472	  reason);
473	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
474	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
475	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
476	
477	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
478	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
479	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
480	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
481	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
482	
483	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
484	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
485	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
486	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
487	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
488	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
489	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
490	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
491	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
492	triggered it.
493	
494	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
495	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
496	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
497	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
498	results as before.
499	
500	### Inspect the delivery history
501	
502	```http
503	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
504	```
505	
506	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
507	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
508	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
509	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
510	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
511	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
512	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
513	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
514	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
515	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
516	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
517	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
518	
519	### Schedules
520	
521	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
522	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
523	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
524	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
525	
526	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
527	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
528	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
529	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
530	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
531	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
532	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
533	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
534	
535	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
536	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
537	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
538	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
539	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
540	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
541	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
542	created is exposed through the status query below.
543	
544	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
545	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
546	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
547	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
548	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
549	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
550	
551	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
552	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
553	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
554	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
555	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
556	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
557	
558	### Declare or replace a schedule
559	
560	```http
561	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
562	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
563	
564	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
565	```
566	
567	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
568	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
569	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
570	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
571	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
572	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
573	
574	### Inspect the schedule status
575	
576	```http
577	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
578	```
579	
580	Returns the declared plan as given (`interval_seconds` or `cron`, the
581	`input`, and the `missed_policy`), whether the schedule is currently
582	`paused`, the `last_triggered_at` time, and the `last_execution_id` of the
583	most recently created execution (both `null` until the first trigger). A
584	workflow that never declared a schedule returns the definite empty result
585	`{"schedule":null}`, and a missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
586	
587	### Pause and resume a schedule
588	
589	```http
590	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
591	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
592	
593	{}
594	```
595	
596	```http
597	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
598	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
599	
600	{}
601	```
602	
603	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
604	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
605	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
606	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
607	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
608	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
609	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
610	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
611	
612	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
613	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
614	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
615	
616	### Checkpoints
617	
618	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
619	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
620	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
621	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
622	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
623	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
624	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
625	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
626	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
627	duplicating any node output.
628	
629	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
630	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
631	same state shape and event stream as before.
632	
633	### Complete the next ready node
634	
635	```http
636	POST /executions/run-1/advance
637	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
638	
639	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
640	```
641	
642	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
643	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
644	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
645	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
646	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
647	the status becomes `completed`.
648	
649	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
650	
651	```http
652	POST /executions/run-1/advance
653	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
654	
655	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
656	```
657	
658	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
659	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
660	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
661	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
662	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
663	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
664	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
665	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
666	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
667	
668	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
669	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
670	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
671	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
672	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
673	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
674	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
675	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
676	the execution stream.
677	
678	### Cancel an execution
679	
680	```http
681	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
682	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
683	```
684	
685	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
686	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
687	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
688	
689	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
690	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
691	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
692	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
693	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
694	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
695	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
696	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
697	
698	### Claim a work item
699	
700	```http
701	POST /executions/run-1/claim
702	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
703	
704	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
705	```
706	
707	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
708	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
709	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
710	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
711	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
712	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
713	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
714	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
715	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
716	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
717	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
718	
719	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
720	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
721	
722	```http
723	POST /executions/run-1/advance
724	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
725	
726	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
727	```
728	
729	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
730	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
731	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
732	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
733	an execution without any claim.
734	
735	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
736	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
737	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
738	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
739	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
740	
741	### Renew a lease
742	
743	```http
744	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
745	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
746	
747	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
748	```
749	
750	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
751	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
752	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
753	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
754	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
755	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
756	
757	### Release a work item
758	
759	```http
760	POST /executions/run-1/release
761	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
762	
763	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
764	```
765	
766	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
767	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
768	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
769	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
770	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
771	`not_found`.
772	
773	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
774	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
775	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
776	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
777	restarts.
778	
779	### Recover from a checkpoint
780	
781	```http
782	POST /executions/run-1/recover
783	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
784	
785	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
786	```
787	
788	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
789	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
790	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
791	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
792	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
793	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
794	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
795	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
796	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
797	execution state and events.
798	
799	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
800	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
801	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
802	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
803	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
804	stays consistent with the materialized state.
805	
806	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
807	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
808	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
809	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
810	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
811	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
812	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
813	
814	### Replay
815	
816	```http
817	POST /executions/run-1/replay
818	```
819	
820	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
821	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
822	and the rebuilt execution.
823	
824	## Errors
825	
826	Errors use this shape:
827	
828	```json
829	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
830	```
831	
832	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
833	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
834	declarations require a tenant and positive integer limits, validated by the
835	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
836	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
837	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
838	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
839	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
840	missing resource (`404 not_found`).
841	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
842	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
843	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
844	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
845	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
846	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
847	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
848	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
849	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
850	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
851	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
852	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
853	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
854	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
855	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
856	A decision by an approver who is
857	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
858	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
859	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
860	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
861	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
862	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
863	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
864	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
865	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
866	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
867	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
868	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
869	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
870	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
871	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
872	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
873	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
874	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
875	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
876	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
877	
878	## Tests
879	
880	```bash
881	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
882	```
883
